17.0.0.en: 1 For great are thy judgments, and cannot be expressed; therefore unnurtured souls have erred. 2 For when the wicked thought to oppress the holy nation, they, being shut up in their houses, the prisoners of darkness and fettered with the bonds of a long night, lay there exiled from the eternal providence. 3 For while they supposed to lie hid in their secret sins, they were scattered under a dark veil of forgetfulness, being horribly astonished, and troubled with apparitions.

17.0.1.en: For great are thy judgments and cannot be expressed; therefore souls that were not disciplined have erred. [1]

17.1.0.en: For when the wicked supposed that they would have dominion over the holy nation, they became prisoners of darkness, bound with a long night, shut up under their roofs, exiled from the eternal providence. [2]

17.1.1.en: The plague of darkness that came upon the Egyptians came before the final plague, “the slaying of the firstborn,” as though it were the last divine warning directed against the wicked so that they might discover what they were and reassess the situation.

17.1.2.en: By this plague the greatness of God’s wisdom appeared, for the following reasons:

17.1.3.en: First: by falling under this plague they perceive the inner darkness that had settled in their hearts and thoughts. Their souls had erred and had paid no heed to the preceding successive plagues, so they became like those in wandering and error, and the features of the true way were lost to them, because they had rejected the divine light. Rightly was it said of them: “Therefore unnurtured souls have erred.”

17.1.4.en: Second: they live in delusion, and do not perceive the truth, so they think that they are possessors of authority, that there is none who can stand before them or repel their assaults upon a defenseless, enslaved people.

17.1.5.en: Third: they mock this defenseless people, and do not perceive that at that time they represent a holy nation.

17.1.6.en: Fourth: these cruel men did not perceive that they were being cruel only to themselves, for they were “prisoners of darkness,” bound and in a long night, upon which perhaps no morning light will dawn because of their stubbornness.

17.1.7.en: Fifth: by their violence and cruelty they became prisoners without iron fetters, in a prison made by their own sins: “shut up under their roofs.”

17.1.8.en: Sixth: since they are without mercy they deprive themselves of God’s mercy and kindness, “exiled from the eternal providence.”

17.1.9.en: These six facts are the making of the sinner who persists in violence, injustice and cruelty: an inner darkness in the depths of the soul; reliance on an imaginary authority that has no existence; failure to perceive the potential of those whom they treat cruelly, and to recognize their true reality; they take themselves captive in darkness without hope of enjoying a shining light; they imprison themselves in a prison made by the work of their own hands; and finally they deprive themselves of the divine mercies.

17.1.10.en: Pharaoh and his men thought that they were possessors of authority with none to restrain them, so they paid no heed to the divine command issued to them through the man of God, Moses. And instead of responding to it, in stubbornness strict orders were issued to treat the people of God with cruelty and violence. And since they persisted in this even after suffering many disciplines, they were struck with the plague of darkness. Here the wise man portrays the Egyptians in prison and darkness, unable to carry on their daily work, and no light was found except in the land of Goshen (today’s Sharqia governorate). Instead of their enslaving the Jews, they imprisoned themselves in their own houses in the midst of pitch darkness, and even the gift of the shining of the material sun left them. It was not possible for their god, as they were worshipping the sun (the god Ra), to deliver them from the darkness.

17.1.11.en: Their houses were turned into an unbearable hell, where phantoms assailed them, and their strength was dissolved by fear.

17.1.12.en: God, the lover of mankind, makes His sun to rise on the evil and on the good (Mt 5:45), and out of His love also He permits this gift to be taken away at times, so that when the wicked man loses the tangible light he may perceive that he has lost the divine light in his depths, and that the evil darkness has dominion over his heart, his mind and his senses! Thus he appears as one who has lost the divine providence (Wis 17:2).

17.1.13.en: * Surely this darkness of the heart is in itself a punishment, that is, blindness of heart, because they abandoned the light of wisdom they fell into graver and graver sins.

17.1.14.en: St. Augustine Origen sees that the darkness points to the plague of ignorance with which the wicked man is struck.

17.1.15.en: * Who was able to break the plague of ignorance, the destroying darkness? Not a prophet, nor an apostle, nor any righteous man! But rather there was need of the power of a God who comes down from heaven, able to die for us all, that by His death we might have a defense against Satan.

17.2.0.en: Origen They supposed that they would remain hidden in their secret sins; they were scattered under the dark veil of forgetfulness, being in great terror, troubled with phantoms. [3]

17.2.1.en: When man commits sin, he thinks that he is acting with wisdom or cunning, and that there is none who can discover his matter. And with the passing of time he reckons that what he did has been folded away by time and has become forgotten. But even if his matter is not discovered among men, and he does not fall under a civil or criminal penalty, he falls under a penalty in his depths. For a great terror comes upon him and a dread of phantoms that pursue him. This is one of the curses that come upon him who falls into evil, as he tries to flee, scattered among many ways, with no enemy behind him following his tracks. The enemy of the sinner is within him, terrifying him, and none can rescue him from it except God Himself, if he returns to Him in repentance. Its remedy is to drive out fear by fear, for the fear that comes without hope from committing sin is removed by the fear of the Lord, which fills the soul with hope in the Savior of the world, the lover and sanctifier of sinners.

17.2.2.en: It is written among the curses that come upon him who is determined to rebel and disobey the divine commandment: “The Lord shall send upon thee cursing, vexation, and rebuke, in all that thou settest thine hand unto for to do, until thou be destroyed, and until thou perish quickly; because of the wickedness of thy doings, whereby thou hast forsaken me” (Deut 28:20). If the fruit of the Spirit is love mingled with joy (Gal 5:23), as the Holy Spirit carries the soul as though to heaven to taste eternal joy while it is still in the midst of the world’s troubles, cares and trials, then the work of sin, especially disobedience, is the deprivation of man of this heavenly atmosphere. For by disobedience man turns his back on God, the source of true joy, so he casts himself into the hell of anxiety and disturbance, bearing a spirit of rebuke and ingratitude in every work to which his hand reaches. He drives himself by himself to inner ruin.

17.2.3.en: The enemy of good is bound to the night and darkness, because he cannot bear the true light. All his works are evil and deceptive, therefore they are counted darkness.

17.2.4.en: * The deception of the enemy is night, as Paul said: [We are not of the night, but of the day] (cf. 1 Thess 5:5-8).

17.2.5.en: St. Mar Isaac the Syrian St. John Chrysostom criticizes the worshippers of idols because they destroyed the light that was in them (the natural law), so they became in darkness.

17.2.6.en: * This is the gravest accusation against the pagans (that they left God), and the second is that they worshipped idols (Jer 2:13)… The pagans tried to reach heaven, but since they destroyed the light that was in them, and instead trusted in themselves, in the darkness of their thinking, they looked for the immaterial in bodies and gazed at the unlimited in created forms, and by this they lost their harmony with the light.

17.2.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * Surely this darkness of the heart was a punishment and a recompense; by this recompense, which is blindness of heart because of abandoning the light of wisdom, they fell into graver and graver sins.

17.3.s.en: 2. No escape from the deadly terror

17.3.0.en: 4 For neither did the corner that held them keep them from fear, but noises as of waters falling down sounded about them, and sad visions appeared unto them with heavy countenances.

17.3.1.en: For the inner chambers that kept them did not shield them from fear, for loud noises resounded about them, and phantoms with appalling faces appeared to them. [4]

17.3.2.en: In some translations it reads: “the nests in which they lodged did not shield them from terror.” So he likens them to young birds lying in nests, thinking that they are protected among the branches of the trees, with none to approach and harm them.

17.3.3.en: What was the refuge that the Egyptians thought able to cover them from what they were committing, except their feeling that they were possessors of authority and that they were above the law?! This feeble refuge was not able to protect them from the terror within them, and the loud noises resounding about them, and the phantoms that terrified them in the midst of the pitch darkness.

17.3.4.en: The matter did not stop at the loss of light and the dominion of darkness over the wicked, but God permitted the apparitions of demons to terrify them in the midst of the darkness, so that they might perceive that they had refused to belong to God and had accepted by their own will sonship to the devil.

17.3.5.en: * If someone constantly thinks about what pleases God and what does not please Him, it may be said of him that the fear of God is always before his eyes. But such a person needs to be tested and to learn diligently in the law of God, so that he may not fear where there is no cause for fear. For the fear of God must always be set before our eyes - not the eyes of the body, for what we are speaking of here is something unseen and immaterial, but the eyes of the mind, where the perception and understanding of the fear of God is clear, and by this, as we said before, we discover what we must fear and what we must not fear. For he who fears God does not fear the rulers of this world.

17.3.6.en: Origen The Egyptians failed to find a refuge for themselves from the darkness; there was need of the intervention of the Holy Spirit to be delivered from it.

17.3.7.en: * We must ask the Lord Himself, the Holy Spirit Himself, to remove every cloud and all the darkness that hinders the sight from our hearts, which have been hardened by the defilement of sins, so that we may behold the knowledge of His wonderful spiritual law.

17.3.8.en: Origen To be rid of the darkness, it befits us to overcome the love of the world, so that we may be occupied with the heavenly things and see them.

17.3.9.en: * No one who has overcome (the love of the world) and been made worthy of the world to come is blind in understanding, because his eyes are enlightened.

17.4.0.en: 5 No power of the fire, however strong, could give them light, neither could the bright flames of the stars enlighten that horrible night. 6 Only there appeared unto them a fire kindled of itself, very dreadful; for being much terrified, they thought the things which they saw to be worse than the sight they saw not.

17.4.1.en: And no fire, however strong its power, gave light, nor did the shining of the stars illumine that murky night. [5]

17.4.2.en: The darkness was a plague for discipline, therefore all their attempts to kindle a fire or lamps, however strong they were, ended in failure.

17.4.3.en: Even with the splendor of the stars, it was not able to illumine the murky night that had come upon them.

17.4.4.en: It was an unnatural darkness; no artificial or natural lights could dispel it. As though the darkness were crying out in a loud voice: there is no salvation for you by any means except by returning to God, the true Light, who alone is able to dispel your inner darkness.

17.4.5.en: And nothing shone for them but masses of fire that kindled of themselves, and cast terror.

17.5.0.en: And when this sight passed away from them, they were still trembling, reckoning that what appeared to them was more dreadful than it was. [6]

17.5.1.en: Masses of fire appeared to them, not to give them light but to terrify them. Perhaps these masses represented fiery evil spirits, but without radiance and unable to give light, or they were from the inspiration of their imaginations. They were in great perplexity, for the pitch darkness terrified them, and the masses of fire did not remedy the matter, but rather inflamed their hearts the more with terror.

17.5.2.en: Perhaps these masses of fire were the work of magic, for the magicians tried to resist the darkness, which was a divine discipline, by producing masses of fire that gave them light. But the masses appeared and were unable to dispel the darkness and remove the fear and terror, which terrified the Egyptians all the more.

17.5.3.en: Since the creation of Adam the enemy of good has exerted every effort to imitate God and His angels so as to catch man in his nets by deception. Here the enemy of good tried - through magic - to appear as masses of fire, so as to assure the Egyptians that he is God.

17.5.4.en: * This is Satan’s habit, to imitate the things that belong to God. He raises up false prophets who resist the true prophets, and he also appears in the form of an angel to deceive men.

17.5.5.en: Father Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus * If we have Christ in our hearts, He gives us light. Therefore if the perception of knowledge removes ignorance, and if we leave unseemly works and do what is upright, then we are in the light, and we walk faithfully as in the day.

17.6.s.en: 4. The inability of magic to remove the darkness

17.6.0.en: 7 Then the art of magic was put down, and their vaunting in wisdom was reproved with disgrace, 8 for they that promised to drive away terrors and troubles from a sick soul were themselves sick of fear, worthy to be laughed at.

17.6.1.en: The trickery of their magic art was powerless, and its claim to wisdom was silenced with disgrace. [7]

17.7.0.en: For those who promised to drive away fears and troubles from the sick soul, these a ridiculous fear made sick. [8]

17.7.1.en: They chose to submit to the powers of darkness, and despised taking refuge under the wings of God (Ps 91:4), so they could not be delivered from the frightening voices of the demons or stop their moving about them. In vain they tried to light a lamp in their houses to protect them from the darkness of the devil, because “Except the Lord keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain” (Ps 127:1).

17.7.2.en: The demons saw the Egyptians resorting to kindling fires to give them light, so they hastened to frighten them by showing themselves as flaming fires in the air, moving before them, and the Egyptians were very afraid.

17.7.3.en: The Egyptians were skilled in magic and relied on it, so that Pharaoh and his counselors thought that they were able to resist Moses and Aaron by means of the magicians. And behold, the demons that play a principal role in magic were unable to rescue them from the plague of darkness that came upon them by divine permission, and instead of offering them help, the demons became an object of greater terror.

17.8.0.en: 9 For though no terrible thing did fear them, yet being scared with beasts that passed by, and hissing of serpents, they were overcome.

17.8.1.en: For though there was no terrible thing to frighten them, the passing of animals and the hissing of serpents alarmed them. [9]

17.8.2.en: How marvelous! Those who used to worship some insects and creeping things, now the little creatures and serpents terrified them in the midst of the darkness.

17.9.0.en: 9 So they perished for fear, and denied that they saw the air, which could of no side be avoided. 10 For wickedness, condemned by her own witness, is very timorous, and being pressed with conscience, always forecasteth grievous things. 11 For fear is nothing else but a betraying of the succours which reason offereth, 12 and the expectation from within, being less, counteth the ignorance more than the cause which bringeth the torment.

17.9.1.en: So they perished from the terrifying fear, and refused even to look at the air, which cannot be avoided. [10]

17.9.2.en: Everything around them, even the air, turned into a source of terror for them, for the inner terror is reflected upon man’s senses, so he thinks that everything around him is exceedingly terrifying and frightening, and he wishes to close his eyes, for he cannot bear to look even at the air he breathes.

17.10.0.en: For wickedness is a mark of cowardice, when it is condemned by its own witness, and under the pressure of conscience it keeps magnifying difficulties. [11]

17.10.1.en: The wise man presents to us a grave truth, namely that terror comes upon man from within, through his wickedness and the crookedness of his heart and its turning away from God, the source of his peace; for sin begets anxiety, and the righteousness of God begets peace and joy.

17.11.0.en: For fear is nothing but the abandonment of the helps of reason. [12]

17.11.1.en: The wise man reveals the cause of fear in the life of the wicked: it is not from events that befall them, nor from circumstances surrounding them, but from their losing the soundness of their minds, so there is no help that can give them rest.

17.11.2.en: * Darkness points to the sins of the flesh, which are practiced through worldly enticements… But to take up the armor of light (Rom 13:12) is to practice good works.

17.12.0.en: Father Ambrosiaster The weaker the expectation of help, the greater the sense of ignorance of what brings the torment. [13]

17.12.1.en: The wicked lose their hope of enjoying balance of mind, for there is no help for the reason, and consequently bitter torment comes upon them through their ignorance of what they are.

17.13.s.en: 7. The darkness of death or the prison of the grave

17.13.0.en: 13 For they that slept the same sleep that night, which was intolerable, and which came upon them out of the bottoms of inevitable hell, 14 were partly vexed with monstrous apparitions, and partly fainted, their heart failing them; for a sudden fear, and not looked for, came upon them. 15 So then whosoever there fell down was straitly kept, shut up in a prison without iron bars.

17.14.0.en: But they, in that night which was truly powerless and which came from the depths of the realm of the dead, were sleeping the very same sleep (of death). [14]

17.14.1.en: Their life was turned into a bitter night, as though it were not the work of nature, like an eclipse of the sun, but issued from hell, to turn their life into hell, as they said. And with their great terror they became like those who slept in the grave and lay down.

17.15.0.en: And at one time dreadful phantoms pursued them, and at another their strength was dissolved by the faintness of their souls, because of the sudden and unexpected fear that came upon them. [15]

17.15.1.en: Finally, their terror has three sources: the phantoms that pursued them, the dissolving of their hearts and their complete collapse, and their failure to perceive what would befall them after that.

17.16.0.en: And so whoever fell there, whoever he was, was kept shut up in a prison without iron. [16]

17.16.1.en: They were in a terrifying prison; they shut themselves up by themselves in their houses, fearing to move inside the house or to go out of it, lest they strike against something in the intensity of the darkness and fall to the ground. The darkness bound them as with chains on their hands and feet, so they were unable to move, so that perhaps they might perceive the state of captivity that had come upon their souls without their knowing.

17.16.2.en: The wicked shut themselves up in the prison of darkness that has no iron. They are terrified by the fear that comes from the inability of their minds to supply them with peace. “They were more grievous unto themselves than the darkness” (Wis 17:20).

17.17.s.en: 8. Bound with one chain of darkness

17.17.0.en: 16 For whether he were husbandman, or shepherd, or a labourer in the field, he was overtaken, and endured that necessity, which could not be avoided; for they were all bound with one chain of darkness. 17 Whether it were a whistling wind, or a melodious noise of birds among the spreading branches, or a pleasing fall of water running violently, 18 or a terrible sound of stones cast down, or a running that could not be seen of skipping beasts, or a roaring voice of most savage wild beasts, or a rebounding echo from the hollow mountains, these things made them to swoon for fear.

17.18.0.en: For whether he was a farmer or a shepherd or one who did a work of the wilderness, he was suddenly seized and fell into the inevitable doom. [17]

17.18.1.en: The darkness came upon them suddenly, so those who were in farming, or tending sheep, or practicing any work in the wilderness were not given a chance to go to their houses, but remained groping in the midst of the darkness, not knowing how to move.

17.18.2.en: For they were all bound with one chain of darkness.

17.19.0.en: For the whistling of the wind, the singing of birds on the spreading branches, and the rhythm of rushing water. [18]

17.20.0.en: And the crashing of tumbling stones, the unseen running of leaping animals, the roaring of the most savage beasts, and the echo resounding in the hollows of the mountains, all this paralyzed them with fear. [19]

17.20.1.en: What added to the terror was that while they were in the captivity of darkness, everything around them increased their anxiety: the sound of the branches of the trees, the rushing water and the tumbling stones, even the animals which in their terror of the darkness ran uncontrolled in a state of hysteria, and so on. All this deprived them of every possibility of reassurance! Their hearts were dissolved, because all nature was in revolt against them, and they feared the attack of the raging beasts of prey. Therefore they stayed in their places in the wildernesses, like those bound with one chain, none daring to move to find a companion in his distress.

17.21.0.en: 19 For the whole world shined with clear light, and none were hindered in their labour. 20 Over them only was spread a heavy night, an image of that darkness which should afterward receive them; but yet were they unto themselves more grievous than the darkness.

17.22.0.en: For the whole world was illumined by a bright light, and carried on its works without hindrance. [20]

17.22.1.en: The whole world was enjoying the gift of God, that is, the existence of day and night: men practice their works in the day through the light of the sun and rest at night, but these became in a perpetual night in the midst of a nature in revolt, with their utter inability to practice any work. The darkness struck them with a kind of paralysis, although their limbs were able to move.

17.22.2.en: But over them alone was spread a heavy night, an image of the darkness prepared to receive them, but they were more grievous unto themselves than the darkness. [21]

17.22.3.en: Had the darkness come upon all mankind, there would have been something of consolation in it, for it would be a general and universal distress; but its coming upon them and not upon others is a severe calamity, making them expect the coming of what is harsher than that.

17.22.4.en: * Behold the mercy and the judgment. Mercy for the elect, who obtain the righteousness of God, and judgment upon the others, who are blind. But the former believe because they wish to believe, while the others did not believe because they do not wish it. Therefore mercy and judgment come according to their (men’s) will.

17.22.6.en: Enlighten my depths, and dispel all darkness in me!

17.22.7.en: * My depths within me cry out to You, O true Light.

17.22.8.en: Sin has corrupted my whole being.

17.22.9.en: Pitch darkness has reigned and settled in my depths.

17.22.10.en: I am no longer able to see.

17.22.11.en: I have become like a dead man in a grave, without movement.

17.22.12.en: My soul has turned into great bitterness!

17.22.13.en: Who can dispel my darkness but You?

17.22.15.en: He turned my life into an unbearable hell!

17.22.16.en: I thought in sin there was pleasure and enjoyment, and behold, I am in misery and deprivation.

17.22.17.en: Phantoms have reigned over my soul.

17.22.18.en: And the sense of deprivation has shattered me.

17.22.19.en: * The darkness corrupted my life; I feared everything around me, as though the whole world had become hostile to me.

17.22.20.en: My depths were filled with deadly phantoms!

17.22.21.en: I am no longer able to draw my breath.

17.22.22.en: * Am I, then, in a prison?

17.22.23.en: It is the making of my evil will.

17.22.24.en: Are my soul and my body, then, bound with chains!

17.22.25.en: I have turned as though into a lifeless thing.

17.22.26.en: All vitality has been lost to me; I have lost all ability to move.

17.22.27.en: * I made every effort but to no avail.

17.22.28.en: Who can set me free but You?

17.22.30.en: Shine in my depths, that I may perceive Your love!

17.22.31.en: I see You stretching out Your hands to embrace me.

17.22.32.en: I perceive Your wonderful longing toward me!

17.22.33.en: I cling to You, for You are my all.

17.22.34.en: Your light shatters every trace of darkness.

17.22.35.en: Your light lifts me up to Your heavens!

17.22.38.en: Though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil!

17.22.39.en: * Yes, shine, O Light, upon every man.

17.22.40.en: Dispel the darkness of the devil, and establish Your Kingdom in every soul.

17.22.41.en: Lift every heart to Your heavens, that it may enjoy Your splendor!

17.22.42.en: Let the heart of every man be enlarged, that he may love the light for all the world!
